summary: Connect the lakefront, Rhône crossings, St Pierre hill and old-town lanes in one ascending route, then return at water level instead of circling the same luxury-shopping blocks.

title: International Geneva & Nations Quarter
summary: Treat the UN and international quarter as an access-controlled institutional visit, then connect the parks and lake only after confirmed entry, security and opening conditions.

title: Carouge, Plainpalais & the Arve
summary: Leave central Geneva for Carouge’s smaller streets, Plainpalais markets and the Arve corridor, using the tram as the spine for a neighborhood-focused half day.

title: Lausanne & Lavaux
summary: Lausanne stacks its station, old city and Ouchy lakefront on different elevations, while Lavaux stretches east along rail lines and vineyard terraces. Use metro and trains to control vertical movement, then choose one vineyard segment rather than chasing every named village.

title: Lausanne Old City & Ouchy
summary: Use Lausanne’s metro to connect the cathedral hill, station level and Ouchy waterfront, making elevation part of the itinerary instead of repeatedly climbing the same slope.

title: Lavaux Vineyard Terraces
summary: Explore Lavaux as a working vineyard landscape linked by regional trains, choosing one terrace walk and a confirmed return station rather than collecting villages along the entire slope.

title: Olympic Museum & Lake Geneva Day
summary: Build a lower-Lausanne day around the Olympic Museum and Ouchy, then add a lake boat only when its timetable creates a useful route rather than a sightseeing obligation.

title: Montreux, Vevey & the Riviera
summary: Montreux and Vevey share a dramatic lake-and-mountain setting but serve different days. Chillon is a fixed historical anchor, Rochers-de-Naye is a weather-sensitive mountain excursion, and Vevey adds a smaller urban scale. The regional train network means you never need to walk the entire Riviera to prove you saw it.

title: Montreux Waterfront & Chillon Castle
summary: Use Montreux’s waterfront as the approach or release from Chillon, with bus, train or a selective walk replacing the urge to cover every kilometer of promenade.

title: Rochers-de-Naye Mountain Railway
summary: Treat Rochers-de-Naye as a weather-gated rail excursion from Montreux, with the lake panorama as the reward and a protected descent as the non-negotiable part.

title: Vevey, Lakeside & Riviera Towns
summary: Use Vevey as the quieter Riviera counterpoint to Montreux, with the lakeside, old streets and one cultural stop connected by rail instead of another long promenade march.

title: Interlaken, Thun & Brienz
summary: Interlaken sits between Lake Thun and Lake Brienz and connects onward to the Jungfrau region. The town itself is convenient but not the strongest reason to spend a whole day. Use it as a base, then decide whether the day belongs to Brienz/Giessbach, Thun/Spiez or the high valleys.

title: Interlaken Base & Harder Kulm
summary: Use Interlaken to organize rail, lake and valley departures, then give the town only the time it earns: a compact walk, logistics reset and optionally Harder Kulm in clear weather.

title: Lake Brienz, Brienz & Giessbach
summary: Choose a boat–rail combination around Lake Brienz, using Brienz or Giessbach as the one main stop and protecting the return rather than trying to hop every pier.

title: Lake Thun, Thun & Spiez
summary: Use the western lake for a town-and-castle day, choosing Thun’s urban old town or Spiez’s compact bay as the main anchor and connecting by rail or boat.

title: Jungfrau Region
summary: Lauterbrunnen, Wengen and Grindelwald look close on a map but each uses a different valley and mountain-rail rhythm. A successful stay separates valley floor, high-village and summit days. The region rewards early starts, weather swaps and disciplined return planning far more than collecting every famous viewpoint.

title: Lauterbrunnen Valley & Mürren
summary: Use Lauterbrunnen as the valley-floor spine, then choose either Mürren/Gimmelwald elevation or a longer waterfall-valley walk rather than trying to stack every cableway.

title: Wengen & Kleine Scheidegg
summary: Climb from Lauterbrunnen to car-free Wengen and, when weather supports it, continue toward Kleine Scheidegg for a mountain-rail day with a clear turnaround point.

title: Grindelwald & First
summary: Use Grindelwald as the base and First as a weather-gated mountain layer, with Bachalpsee or ridge walking added only when trails and return time support it.

title: Zermatt & the Matterhorn
summary: Zermatt’s car-free village concentrates rail, mountain transport and Matterhorn viewpoints into a small valley head. The challenge is not access to options but choosing one elevation system per day. Use village time as the buffer around mountain weather, not as a fourth attraction squeezed between summit tickets.

title: Zermatt Village & Gornergrat
summary: Pair a compact village orientation with Gornergrat only when the Matterhorn and surrounding peaks are likely to be visible, then use the cogwheel line as the day’s main elevation system.

title: Sunnegga & Five Lakes
summary: Use the Sunnegga side for a lighter high-altitude day, choosing a short viewpoint circuit or the Five Lakes route only after checking trail condition, heat and cloud.

title: Matterhorn Glacier Paradise
summary: Treat Matterhorn Glacier Paradise as an altitude excursion with cable-car dependencies, not simply the next Matterhorn viewpoint; health, wind and visibility decide whether it belongs in the plan.

title: St Moritz & Upper Engadin
summary: St Moritz is the transport and hotel anchor, but the Upper Engadin’s identity stretches through lakes, Pontresina and the Bernina corridor. Distances are modest by rail yet elevation and winter conditions remain real. Choose one landscape system per day instead of repeatedly returning to St Moritz between every stop.

title: St Moritz & Engadin Lakes
summary: Use St Moritz as the base but let the lake chain define the day, moving by rail/bus between viewpoints and villages rather than walking every shoreline.

title: Pontresina & Bernina Railway
summary: Ride the Bernina corridor as a real rail journey through changing elevation, choosing one turnaround or stop rather than treating every station as a photo target.

title: Muottas Muragl, Pontresina & Diavolezza
summary: Choose one Engadin high viewpoint by scale and effort: Muottas Muragl for valley geometry or Diavolezza for glacier-facing high terrain, then keep Pontresina as the base layer.

title: Chur, Davos & Graubünden
summary: Chur is a compact historic city and the practical gate to multiple Rhaetian Railway corridors. Davos, Arosa and the Rhine Gorge are not neighboring attractions in walking terms; each is a distinct rail or road day. Treat the canton as a set of transport corridors with different weather and seasonal functions.

title: Chur Old Town & Rhine Gorge
summary: Use Chur’s old town as a compact urban anchor, then choose a specific Rhine Gorge rail or walking segment rather than treating the entire gorge as one roadside viewpoint.

title: Davos & Parsenn
summary: Treat Davos as a high-valley base whose useful plan changes by season, then choose Parsenn or a lower lake/valley day according to lift status and weather.

title: Arosa & the Mountain Railway
summary: Make the Chur–Arosa railway part of the excursion, then keep the resort day focused on the lake, village or one open mountain area rather than chasing multiple lift systems.

title: Lugano & Southern Ticino
summary: Lugano is compact around the lake but steep once the hills begin. Monte San Salvatore, Monte Brè and Monte Generoso are separate viewpoint systems with different access. The city works best when one elevation choice supports a lakeside day rather than becoming a checklist of summits.

title: Lugano Center & Lakefront
summary: Connect Lugano station, historic center, Parco Ciani and lakefront in one downhill city sequence, then use transit for the return climb instead of retracing it.

title: Monte San Salvatore & Morcote
summary: Use Monte San Salvatore for the overhead lake view, then choose Morcote as a separate village chapter reached by public transport rather than an improvised long ridge traverse.

title: Mendrisiotto & Monte Generoso
summary: Leave Lugano by regional rail for Mendrisiotto and Monte Generoso only when the mountain railway and weather align, keeping the district as a distinct southern-Ticino day.

title: Locarno, Ascona & Ticino Valleys
summary: Locarno and Ascona form a relaxed lake base, while Verzasca, Maggia and Centovalli branch away with different bus and rail logic. The valleys are not interchangeable Instagram stops: water level, heat, trail condition and transport frequency should decide which one fits.

title: Locarno & Ascona Lakefront
summary: Treat Locarno and Ascona as complementary lake towns linked by bus or boat, giving each a different role instead of walking the suburban gap simply because they share the basin.

title: Verzasca Valley
summary: Use the valley bus as the spine, choose one village and one river section, and treat water conditions as a primary safety decision rather than a backdrop to the stone bridge.

title: Maggia Valley & Centovalli
summary: Choose between a bus-based Maggia valley day and the rail-based Centovalli corridor; both reveal Ticino beyond the lake, but they solve different travel days.

title: Schaffhausen & Rhine Falls
summary: Rhine Falls is easy to reach but confusing when treated as a single pin. The north and south banks offer different access and attraction patterns, while Schaffhausen and Stein am Rhein add urban depth. Choose the fall bank before arrival and keep the city visit from becoming only a lunch stop.

title: Rhine Falls: Choose the Right Bank
summary: Plan Rhine Falls by bank, rail stop and desired viewpoint, then cross or transfer only when the second side adds something meaningful.

title: Schaffhausen Old Town & Munot
summary: Give Schaffhausen its own compact loop through painted facades, arcades and Munot, rather than using the city only as a rail interchange for Rhine Falls.

title: Stein am Rhein & Upper Rhine
summary: Use regional rail to reach Stein am Rhein for its painted old town and river edge, then return without turning the day into a chain of tiny border towns.

title: St Gallen & Appenzell
summary: St Gallen’s Abbey District, Appenzell’s compact village and the Alpstein mountains form three different travel modes within a short regional network. The key is not distance but elevation: culture and village days remain robust when the high trails or cable car are in cloud.

title: St Gallen Abbey District & Old Town
summary: Build St Gallen around the Abbey District and its library context, then use the old town’s oriel windows and compact streets as a supporting urban chapter.
keywords: St Gallen Abbey District & Old Town

title: Appenzell Village & Rolling Country
summary: Use Appenzell village as a compact cultural center, then add one signed countryside walk instead of treating private farms and painted houses as an open-air theme park.

title: Ebenalp & Seealpsee
summary: Treat Ebenalp and Seealpsee as mountain terrain with a cable-car access point, choosing viewpoint, cave path or lake hike only when trails and weather are suitable.

title: France Travel Guide
summary: Plan France through twenty complete regional hubs and sixty focused guides for cities, palaces, vineyards, coasts, mountains and Corsica.

title: Paris
summary: Paris works best as a set of walkable river and neighborhood fields joined by short Métro or RER moves. The useful decision is not how many landmarks fit on a map, but which timed interior anchors the day and which streets, gardens and river crossings form a coherent approach and exit.

title: Seine Islands & the Latin Quarter
summary: Use one reserved interior on the island, cross once into the Latin Quarter, and finish along a different Seine edge so the oldest part of Paris reads as connected ground rather than a queue of monuments.

title: Louvre, Tuileries & the Opéra Axis
summary: Anchor the day at one museum entrance, move west through courtyards and the Tuileries, and turn north only once toward Palais Royal, the covered passages or Palais Garnier.

title: Eiffel Tower, Invalides & Western Views
summary: Treat the Eiffel Tower as a ticketed operating system, not a photo stop, then choose either military history, Seine space or a separate skyline view as the day’s second argument.

title: Versailles, Fontainebleau & Giverny
summary: The famous excursions around Paris use different rail terminals, local transfers, reservation systems and landscape scales. Treat Versailles, Fontainebleau and Giverny as three separate operating days rather than interchangeable palace cards.

title: Versailles Palace & Estate
summary: Use a timed palace entry as one contract, then choose either the main gardens or the Trianon estate as the second; the scale between them is the planning fact most day trips miss.

title: Fontainebleau Palace & Forest Edge
summary: Fontainebleau offers a denser royal interior than a casual day-trip label suggests; reserve attention for the palace, then add either town streets or a defined forest edge with a known return.

title: Giverny, Monet’s Gardens & Vernon
summary: Build backward from the Vernon–Giverny connection and the foundation ticket, then decide whether Vernon town or a slower village walk is worth the remaining transport margin.

title: Lille, Arras & the Opal Coast
summary: Lille is a rail gateway to three very different northern trips: Flemish-influenced city streets and collections, First World War remembrance landscapes around Arras, and weather-exposed Channel headlands. Each uses a different last mile and deserves its own day.

title: Old Lille, La Piscine & Roubaix
summary: Walk Lille’s civic and Flemish-influenced core as one compact loop, then use the Métro or tram for a deliberate Roubaix collection block only when its opening and return fit.

title: Arras, Vimy & Remembrance Ground
summary: Use Arras as the civic and rail anchor, then visit Vimy or another defined remembrance site through an official tour, taxi, bicycle plan or car route whose return is already fixed.

title: Opal Coast Headlands & Boulogne
summary: Use Boulogne-sur-Mer, Calais or a smaller coast base according to the chosen headland, then match one exposed walk with one sheltered town or marine visit.

title: Normandy: Rouen, Bayeux & Mont-Saint-Michel
summary: Normandy’s best-known places lie on different rail and road systems: Rouen is a compact Seine city, Bayeux is a base for interpreted D-Day landscapes, and Mont-Saint-Michel is a tidal monument with a controlled final approach. They are not one Paris day-trip chain.

title: Rouen Cathedral, Old Streets & the Seine
summary: Start at the cathedral quarter, cross the Gros-Horloge and market area, then finish at the Seine or a collection that explains the city’s art, Joan of Arc history or wartime layers.

title: Bayeux & the D-Day Landscape
summary: Separate Bayeux’s medieval and museum day from a coast circuit, then build the D-Day route around a defined theme, respectful site conduct and a dependable return.

title: Mont-Saint-Michel & the Bay Approach
summary: Treat the mainland arrival, shuttle or walk, village climb and abbey as four separate layers, then protect the bus, train or parking return before lingering for changing light.

title: Brittany: Walled Ports, Megaliths & Atlantic Headlands
summary: Brittany is not one coastal loop. Saint-Malo and Dinan form a rail-and-bus pair, Carnac and the Gulf of Morbihan revolve around megaliths and boat or local connections, while Quimper and Crozon require a western-base decision. Tides and wind alter each system differently.

title: Loire Valley Châteaux
summary: The Loire Valley is a chain of towns, rail stops, gardens and estates rather than one castle park. Blois and Chambord, Amboise and Chenonceau, and Tours with the western gardens each create a different transport day. Two well-matched sites usually beat a three-château sprint.

title: Blois & Chambord
summary: Read the Château Royal de Blois as an urban palace, then give Chambord’s monumental house and forest estate a separate transport and walking envelope.

title: Amboise, Clos Lucé & Chenonceau
summary: Amboise rewards a town-based royal narrative; Chenonceau rewards a focused estate visit from its nearby station. Link them only when one Amboise interior is deliberately omitted.

title: Tours, Villandry & Azay-le-Rideau
summary: Tours supplies food, rail and city context; Villandry is a garden contract and Azay-le-Rideau is a town-and-château rail branch. Each earns a different schedule.

title: Reims, Épernay & Champagne Country
summary: Champagne travel combines cathedral cities, working cellars, regulated tastings and vineyard villages. Reims and Épernay are rail-friendly bases, while rural producers and southern Champagne need appointments or a clear last mile. Alcohol tasting also changes who can drive.

title: Reims Cathedral & Cellar Districts
summary: Use the cathedral and Palais du Tau context in the center, then travel to one house whose tour language, time and tasting conditions are confirmed.

title: Épernay, Avenue de Champagne & Vineyard Villages
summary: The Avenue de Champagne is walkable from town; the vineyards are not a free-form extension. One booked house plus one safely reached village creates the useful day.
keywords: Épernay, Avenue de Champagne & Vineyard Villages

title: Troyes & Southern Champagne
summary: Troyes is not a consolation stop after Reims: its compact medieval streets, churches and museums support a complete city route before any vineyard transfer.

title: Strasbourg, Colmar & the Alsace Wine Route
summary: Strasbourg and Colmar are strong rail cities with different urban rhythms; the wine-route villages sit on a patchwork of trains, buses, bicycles and roads. A useful Alsace trip separates city depth from a village circuit and does not reduce living communities to façades.
keywords: Strasbourg, Colmar & the Alsace Wine Route

title: Strasbourg Grande Île & European Quarter
parent: Strasbourg, Colmar & the Alsace Wine Route
summary: Walk Grande Île by cathedral, canals and civic streets, then use one tram move for either the Neustadt or European Quarter as the second urban layer.
keywords: Strasbourg, Colmar & the Alsace Wine Route

title: Colmar Canals, Old Town & Museums
parent: Strasbourg, Colmar & the Alsace Wine Route
summary: Use the Unterlinden Museum or another selected interior as the attention anchor, then connect the old town and canal without repeating the same crowded lanes.
keywords: Strasbourg, Colmar & the Alsace Wine Route

title: Alsace Wine Route Villages

summary: Use Sélestat, Colmar or another rail gateway to reach one village pair, one walk and one reserved producer, with the return fixed before tasting.
keywords: Strasbourg, Colmar & the Alsace Wine Route

title: Dijon, Beaune & Burgundy
summary: Burgundy’s “climats” are working vineyard parcels, not a single attraction road. Dijon and Beaune are rail-connected city bases; the Route des Grands Crus and abbey hills require a bicycle, tour, car or rural connection plus responsible tasting decisions.

title: Dijon Ducal City & Markets
summary: Follow the compact center from station to ducal palace, choose one collection, and use market or gastronomy stops without turning branded foods into the whole story.

title: Beaune Hospices & Vineyard Edge
summary: The Hospices provide the civic and medical-history center; a booked cellar or signed vineyard walk becomes the second layer, not a string of anonymous tastings.

title: Vézelay, Fontenay & Abbey Country
summary: Vézelay is a pilgrimage hill with a steep village approach; Fontenay is a secluded Cistercian domain. Each deserves its own last mile, quiet reading and return.

title: Lyon & the Rhône Gateway
summary: Lyon’s planning logic comes from the Saône, Rhône and two hills. Vieux Lyon and Fourvière form a vertical historic route; Presqu’île and Croix-Rousse connect commerce to silk-worker history; Beaujolais and Pérouges require separate regional last miles. Choose the hill before the meal reservation so the final descent, not fatigue, decides where the evening ends.

title: Vieux Lyon & Fourvière
summary: Read the Saône-side old town at street level, take the funicular or a deliberate climb once, and descend by a different safe route with the Roman or basilica layer clearly chosen.

title: Presqu’île, Croix-Rousse & the Silk City
summary: Begin between the rivers, climb by Métro or signed slope to the canut district, and use silk history to explain the urban form rather than treating traboules as a scavenger hunt.

title: Beaujolais Villages or Pérouges
summary: Beaujolais needs a sober vineyard route and appointments; Pérouges needs the correct regional stop and a cobbled hill approach. The two branches answer different interests.

title: Annecy, Chamonix & the French Alps
summary: Annecy, Chamonix and Grenoble expose three different Alpine systems: a lake city with busy shores, a high-mountain valley whose lifts are weather-dependent, and an urban basin opening into Chartreuse and Vercors. A clear valley forecast does not guarantee a useful summit day.

title: Annecy Old Town & Lake
summary: Use the Thiou canals and old streets early, then choose a western-shore walk, a booked boat or a bounded bicycle section whose return works in heat and traffic.

title: Chamonix Mountain Systems
summary: Chamonix is a valley of separate transport products, not one summit ticket. Pay for the system that matches conditions and keep a complete lower-valley day ready.

title: Grenoble, Bastille & Chartreuse Edge
summary: Cross the historic center and Isère, ascend once to the Bastille by cable car or foot, and decide whether the city or a separate lower-mountain excursion carries the afternoon.

title: Bordeaux, Saint-Émilion & Arcachon
summary: Bordeaux’s tram city, Saint-Émilion’s vineyard hill and Arcachon Bay’s dune-and-tide landscape are three complete systems. Regional trains make each reachable, but cellar appointments, dune access and bay boats still require separate decisions.

title: Bordeaux Riverfront & Wine City
summary: Start in the stone center, cross the market and quays once, then choose the Cité du Vin, Bassins des Lumières or a central collection as the day’s main interior.

title: Saint-Émilion Village & Vineyards
summary: The village, monolithic-church context and vineyards form one steep landscape; a booked producer or official tour gives it structure and determines the last mile.

title: Arcachon Bay & Dune du Pilat
summary: Use the train to Arcachon, read wind and access status, and choose one bay contract plus one town layer; the dune is a moving natural site, not a fixed staircase attraction.

title: Dordogne & Périgord Noir
summary: Sarlat’s market city, the Vézère’s prehistoric sites and the Dordogne’s cliff villages and castles are close on a map but dispersed across rural roads. A car, driver, bicycle or arranged tour often determines what is responsible and possible. Build each day inside one valley so a missed cave slot, river shuttle or castle closing does not trigger a long corrective drive.

title: Sarlat Market & Old Town
summary: Enter before the densest market period, trace civic lanes and one viewpoint or museum, then use Sarlat as the meal and transport anchor for the region.

title: Vézère Valley Prehistory
summary: Use Les Eyzies or Montignac as the valley anchor, distinguish original art from facsimile interpretation, and avoid claiming that several timed caves can be improvised in one day.

title: Dordogne Valley Castles & Cliff Villages
summary: Use Beynac, Castelnaud, La Roque-Gageac or Domme as a coherent bank-and-height route, then add canoeing only when water, operator and return conditions are suitable.

title: Toulouse, Albi & Carcassonne
summary: Toulouse’s Garonne and aerospace layers, Albi’s episcopal brick city and Carcassonne’s fortified cité are distinct destinations on separate rail corridors. Both excursions are possible from Toulouse, but neither should be reduced to a two-hour photo stop.

title: Toulouse Garonne & Aerospace Choices
summary: Walk the Capitole–Saint-Sernin–Garonne core as one route, then select Cité de l’espace, Aeroscopia or Halle de La Machine only when its distinct location and admission fit.

title: Albi Episcopal City & Toulouse-Lautrec
summary: Walk from the station into the brick core, give Sainte-Cécile and the Toulouse-Lautrec Museum separate attention, then finish along the Tarn and return through a different street line.

title: Carcassonne Cité & Bastide
summary: Start in the lower town or at the station, cross the Aude and enter the Cité once, then leave enough attention for the lived Bastide rather than spending the whole day inside souvenir lanes.

title: French Basque Coast & the Pyrenees
summary: Bayonne and Biarritz share an urban coastal network, Saint-Jean-de-Luz opens a different harbor and inland Basque corridor, and Gavarnie or Cauterets require a separate Pyrenean base. Ocean conditions and mountain conditions must be checked independently.

title: Bayonne & Biarritz
summary: Walk one complete center first, use bus or rail for the second, and treat ocean safety as a live condition rather than a postcard assumption.

title: Saint-Jean-de-Luz & Basque Inland Villages
summary: The protected bay and fishing-port history differ from Biarritz’s surf coast; Sare, Espelette or another inland stop should be chosen for a specific cultural or landscape reason.

title: Gavarnie, Cauterets & Pyrenean Gateways
summary: Gavarnie and Cauterets open different valleys; Lourdes can be the rail gateway, but the mountain day begins only after the last bus or road connection is solved.

title: Montpellier, Nîmes & the Camargue
summary: Montpellier, Nîmes and Arles sit on a strong rail corridor, but the Pont du Gard, Camargue wetlands and coast require distinct buses, bicycles, tours or cars. Roman monuments, living cities and protected lagoons should not be collapsed into one hot-weather checklist.

title: Montpellier & Sète
summary: Walk Montpellier from Écusson to one tram-served modern district, or take a direct train to Sète for canals, market and Mont Saint-Clair; a two-city day must stay selective.

title: Nîmes & Pont du Gard
summary: Use the Arena, Maison Carrée and Jardins de la Fontaine as one city line; the aqueduct is a separate rural site whose last bus and heat exposure determine the pairing.

title: Arles & the Camargue
summary: Arles’s monuments and Rhône streets deserve their own circuit; the Camargue is a living wetland and agricultural region, not a guaranteed flamingo-and-horse drive-by.

title: Avignon, Aix & the Luberon
summary: Avignon and Aix-en-Provence are independent city bases with different station and street logic. The Luberon’s villages, abbeys and seasonal landscapes require a bus, bicycle, tour or car; market calendars and summer roads shape what is possible.

title: Avignon Papal City & Rhône Edge
summary: Enter through the walls from Avignon Centre, anchor the day on the papal palace or museums, then finish at the Rhône without looping back through every commercial lane.

title: Aix Markets & Cézanne Ground
summary: Walk Cours Mirabeau, the old city and one market or museum, then add Atelier de Cézanne or another verified site without assuming every studio and quarry is open.

title: Luberon Villages & Sénanque
summary: Gordes, Roussillon, Lourmarin and the abbey lie on different road branches. A useful day selects two compatible stops, one meal and a sober, heat-aware return.

title: Marseille, Calanques & Cassis
summary: Marseille’s port city, the Calanques National Park and Cassis–La Ciotat coast meet geographically but operate differently. Urban transit, summer reservations, fire closures, boat conditions and trail difficulty must be checked before choosing the route. Decide between city, land and sea before breakfast; switching access modes late can strand the return at the wrong port or trailhead.

title: Old Port, Le Panier & Mucem
summary: Start at the Vieux-Port, climb once through Le Panier, cross Fort Saint-Jean into Mucem, then return along the water without repeating the same lanes.

title: Calanques Access: Hike, Boat or Shore
summary: A Sugiton reservation, a signed Marseille-side trail, a Cassis approach and a licensed boat are different products; the safest useful day commits to one.
keywords: Calanques Access: Hike, Boat or Shore

title: Cassis, Cap Canaille & La Ciotat
summary: Cassis offers a compact port and Calanques gateway; La Ciotat offers a larger working waterfront and cinema history. Their stations sit away from the postcard centers.

title: Nice & the Côte d’Azur
summary: Nice is a complete city base; the eastern coast toward Èze, Monaco and Menton and the western coast toward Antibes and Cannes form two separate rail and bus directions. Cliff villages require an additional vertical transfer beyond the coastal station.

title: Nice Old Town, Promenade & Hills
summary: Begin at the market and old town, use Castle Hill or Cimiez as the elevation choice, then return by tram or a different shore line.

title: Èze, Monaco & Menton
summary: Èze Village sits high above Èze-sur-Mer; Monaco is a vertical city inside a small territory; Menton is a separate garden-and-old-town stop. One transfer problem should lead the day.

title: Antibes & Cannes West Coast
summary: Use TER to link the towns, give Antibes walls and one collection or Cannes old quarter and film-city context the longer block, then return without a beach-and-island overload.

title: Corsica: Ajaccio, Cap Corse & the South
summary: Corsica’s airports, ferry ports, rail lines and mountain roads create several separate island systems. Ajaccio and the west coast, Bastia and Cap Corse, and Bonifacio–Porto-Vecchio in the south each deserve a base. Driving time, parking and weather outweigh straight-line distance.
keywords: Corsica: Ajaccio, Cap Corse & the South

title: Ajaccio & the West Coast
parent: Corsica: Ajaccio, Cap Corse & the South
summary: Ajaccio’s center, market and Napoleonic context form one city route; the red-cliff west coast is a separate long road or sea day with limited shortcuts.
keywords: Corsica: Ajaccio, Cap Corse & the South

title: Bastia & Cap Corse
parent: Corsica: Ajaccio, Cap Corse & the South
summary: Bastia provides ferry, rail and urban context; Cap Corse is a narrow, slow peninsula whose villages and headlands cannot be collected in a quick loop.

title: Bonifacio & Porto-Vecchio South
parent: Corsica: Ajaccio, Cap Corse & the South

title: United Kingdom Travel Guide
summary: Plan the United Kingdom through twenty complete regional hubs and sixty focused guides for cities, castles, coasts, mountains, islands and Northern Ireland.

title: London
summary: London is not one compact centre but a chain of walkable districts joined by rail, Underground, bus and river services. A useful plan fixes one timed interior, reads the correct station exit and keeps the rest of the day on a coherent street or river line instead of repeatedly crossing the city.

title: Westminster & the South Bank
summary: Start at the booked Westminster door, read Parliament Square and the abbey precinct, then use one bridge to finish along the South Bank with a direct return from Waterloo or Blackfriars.

title: Bloomsbury, the British Museum & Covent Garden
summary: Enter the museum with a bounded collection plan, reset in Bloomsbury, and move south through a single street sequence toward Seven Dials and Covent Garden.
keywords: Bloomsbury, the British Museum & Covent Garden

title: Tower of London, the City & Greenwich
summary: Start with the controlled fortress or a City walk, move east by rail or river only after the anchor, and finish around Greenwich’s compact maritime sites with the return already selected.
keywords: Tower of London, the City & Greenwich

title: Oxford, Blenheim & the Cotswolds
summary: Oxford is a rail-connected walking city, while Blenheim Palace and the Cotswold towns depend on buses, tours, bicycles or a car. A strong base plan distinguishes college opening windows from rural timetables and never treats “the Cotswolds” as one station or one attraction.

title: Oxford Colleges, Libraries & Museums
summary: Start from the railway station or Gloucester Green, confirm the booked or open college, connect Bodleian and Radcliffe Square, then finish with one museum or river edge.

title: Blenheim Palace & Woodstock
summary: Leave Oxford on a verified service, enter through the correct Blenheim gate, choose palace depth or landscape distance, and protect the return from Woodstock before evening frequency changes.

title: Cotswold Towns Without a Car
summary: Select a rail gateway and one or two connected towns, keep the route inside the published bus pattern, and treat footpaths or a tour as separate products rather than invisible links.

title: Cambridge & East Anglia
summary: Cambridge, Ely and Norwich sit on useful rail lines, but their stations, historic cores and surrounding fen or coast landscapes operate at different scales. A good plan distinguishes a walkable academic city from a cathedral stop and a wider East Anglian excursion with its own onward connection.

title: Cambridge Colleges & the Backs
summary: Walk from station to the historic core, meet one verified college gate, continue along public streets and the Backs, and decide separately whether punting or a museum deserves the final block.

title: Ely Cathedral & the Fen Edge
summary: Climb from Ely station and riverside to the cathedral precinct, give the interior a defined block, then choose Oliver Cromwell context or a signed lowland walk before returning downhill.

title: Norwich & a North Norfolk Branch
summary: Walk Norwich’s castle-to-cathedral spine first, then either keep the complete city day or use one verified rail or bus branch with its final return protected.

title: Bath, Bristol & Somerset
summary: Bath and Bristol are close by rail but reward different days: one concentrates Roman archaeology and Georgian streets, the other a working harbour, collections and steep neighbourhoods. Wells, Glastonbury and the Mendips introduce bus-dependent rural connections that should not be hidden inside a city itinerary.

title: Bath: Roman & Georgian City
summary: Begin at Bath Spa, complete one booked central interior, climb through Queen Square and the Circus only if energy allows, and return by a different street line.

title: Bristol Harbourside & Clifton
summary: Start at Temple Meads or the centre, read the working harbour through one museum or ship, then either finish around Clifton or stay with the water and city centre.

title: Wells, Glastonbury & the Mendip Edge
summary: Leave Bath or Bristol on a verified route, give one town and its major site enough time, then use the second place or Mendip landscape only when the onward and return connections are secure.

title: Cornwall & Devon
summary: Cornwall and Devon contain rail-linked cities and harbour towns, but the peninsula’s headlands, villages and moors depend on slower branches, buses, boats or roads. A useful trip chooses a compact base and one weather-facing landscape each day rather than measuring success by the number of coastal names reached.

title: St Ives & the Penwith Coast
summary: Arrive by the branch line, give St Ives harbour and one collection a coherent block, then use a verified bus or bounded coastal walk only when the return and weather remain secure.

title: Falmouth Harbour & the Roseland
summary: Arrive on the correct Falmouth branch station, use the maritime museum or Pendennis as the fixed anchor, then cross the estuary only with a verified outward and return sailing.

title: Exeter & the Dartmoor Edge
summary: Read Exeter’s cathedral and quays first, then remain in the city or commit to one verified moor gateway with weather, daylight and the final rail return already checked.

title: Kent, Sussex & the South Coast
summary: Brighton, Canterbury, Dover and the Seven Sisters sit on different rail and bus corridors despite sharing the south-east coast. A useful day chooses one urban or landscape argument, names the station and final connection, and treats exposed chalk paths as weather decisions rather than scenic filler.

title: Brighton Lanes, Pavilion & Seafront
summary: Descend from Brighton station through the North Laine or Pavilion precinct, complete one interior, then finish on a bounded seafront section with the uphill return already planned.

title: Canterbury Cathedral & Dover Castle
summary: Begin in Canterbury’s walkable core or at Dover’s hillside fortress, complete one deep visit, and add the second place only as a bounded exterior or shorter stop with its return protected.

title: Seven Sisters & Eastbourne
summary: Arrive at a rail-and-bus gateway, read wind and path conditions, complete one signed chalk-coast segment, and turn back or exit before daylight and the final connection become tight.

title: Birmingham & the West Midlands
summary: Birmingham’s canals, civic centre and Jewellery Quarter form a connected urban day, while Stratford-upon-Avon and Ironbridge require different rail or bus corridors and separate heritage bookings. The region works best from one base with one clearly chosen outward branch per day.

title: Birmingham Canals & Jewellery Quarter
summary: Exit the correct central station, read the civic core, follow one canal line to Gas Street and Brindleyplace, then use tram or a deliberate walk to the Jewellery Quarter.

title: Stratford-upon-Avon & Shakespeare
summary: Walk from the station into the birthplace and market-town core, continue to the river and theatre, then protect the train return or performance exit before adding another historic property.

title: Ironbridge Gorge & Shrewsbury
summary: Use Shrewsbury or Telford as the rail gateway, complete one museum cluster or town circuit, and avoid assuming the gorge’s sites form a short walk from a single station.

title: Peak District & Derbyshire
summary: The Peak District is a group of valleys, moors, towns and estates rather than one arrival point. Hope Valley rail, Bakewell and Chatsworth buses, and the southern dales create different day systems. Every plan needs a named gateway, surface-aware route and protected return.

title: Bakewell & Chatsworth
summary: Begin at Bakewell or the estate gate, complete one defined Chatsworth product, and use the town only when the return corridor and daylight remain protected.

title: Hope Valley & Edale
summary: Arrive at Edale, Hope or another chosen station, read the weather from the valley, complete one signed route with a firm turn-back, and reach the railhead before service gaps matter.

title: Dovedale & Ashbourne
summary: Reach Ashbourne or the named valley approach, assess river and path conditions, complete one out-and-back or bounded dale route, and return before the rural connection thins.

title: Liverpool, Manchester & Chester
summary: Liverpool and Manchester are close by rail but their useful visitor geographies point in different directions: Mersey waterfront and mercantile streets versus canals, civic collections and industrial quarters. Chester adds a compact walled city on another line. Each deserves a separate day even when journey times look short.

title: Liverpool Waterfront & Cathedrals
summary: Walk from Lime Street toward the waterfront, use one museum cluster, then climb once toward the cathedrals or remain with the Mersey and finish near a direct station.

title: Manchester Industrial City & Collections
summary: Begin at the station serving the chosen district, use one major collection, connect a bounded canal or civic route, and finish on the same tram or rail side.

title: Chester Walls & Roman City
summary: Walk from Chester station to a named wall gate, complete a weather-aware section or full circuit, descend once for the Rows and one interior, then return through the compact centre.

title: York, Leeds & Yorkshire
summary: York’s walls and Minster, Leeds and Saltaire’s civic-industrial collections, and the North York Moors–Whitby line are three distinct travel systems. Fast intercity rail makes the cities easy to pair across nights, but moor and coast branches need their own weather, heritage-rail and return decisions.

title: York Walls, Minster & Medieval Core
summary: Walk from York station to a named wall gate, complete one coherent wall section, meet the Minster or museum booking, and leave through a different gate toward the station.

title: Leeds Collections & Saltaire
summary: Begin at Leeds station for markets, arcades or a museum, then take one verified local train to Saltaire only when the mill, village and return have a useful time window.

title: Whitby & the North York Moors
summary: Reach Whitby or a moor gateway by the confirmed rail, bus or heritage service, complete one town-and-landscape line, and protect the final return before evening frequency falls away.

title: Lake District & Cumbria
summary: Windermere and Ambleside, Keswick and Derwentwater, and Carlisle with the western Wall use different railheads and buses. The Lake District rewards one basin at a time: weather, boat operation, valley traffic and the last bus matter more than the short distances shown on a map.

title: Windermere, Bowness & Ambleside
summary: Arrive at Windermere station, descend to Bowness or connect to Ambleside, use one verified boat or shore line, and protect the final bus or branch train.

title: Keswick & Derwentwater
summary: Arrive by the confirmed bus, use Keswick as the service base, complete one water or fell branch, and return to the town before the onward bus window narrows.

title: Carlisle & Hadrian’s Wall West
summary: Begin with Carlisle Castle or city context, take one verified corridor to a western fort or wall section, and return before rural frequency and daylight narrow.

title: Newcastle, Durham & Northumberland
summary: Newcastle–Gateshead and Durham are compact rail cities with strong river and collection routes, while Bamburgh and Holy Island introduce long road links and a tidal causeway. The region works when city days remain complete and the coast is planned as a separate weather-and-tide operation.

title: Newcastle & Gateshead Quays
summary: Descend from Newcastle Central through the historic core, use one Quayside collection, cross once to Gateshead, and return by Metro or a different bridge.

title: Durham Cathedral & River Peninsula
summary: Descend from Durham station, climb to Palace Green for one controlled interior, follow one side of the River Wear, and return without repeating the peninsula slopes.

title: Bamburgh Castle & Holy Island
summary: Leave the rail corridor with a named bus, tour or car plan, complete one castle or island visit, and cross the Holy Island causeway only within the official safe window.

title: Edinburgh & the Lothians
summary: Edinburgh’s Old Town ridge, New Town terraces and lower valleys create a vertical city where short map distances conceal stairs and steep streets. East Lothian adds a separate coast railway. A strong plan fixes one controlled interior and uses the city’s level changes as the route rather than an inconvenience.

title: Old Town, Castle & Royal Mile
summary: Enter the Old Town at the correct level, complete one controlled interior, descend the Royal Mile through selected closes, and finish at Holyrood or Waverley without retracing.

title: New Town, Galleries & Dean Village
summary: Start near Princes Street or the gallery complex, walk one New Town terrace line, descend once to Dean Village, and leave through Stockbridge or a planned climb.

title: North Berwick & East Lothian
summary: Walk from North Berwick station to town and harbour, assess wind and sea state, complete one coast activity, and return before the branch service or daylight narrows.

title: Glasgow & the Clyde
summary: Glasgow’s centre, Merchant City and Clyde waterfront form one urban field; the West End has its own museum-and-park rhythm; Loch Lomond adds a rail-to-water branch beyond the city. A useful stay chooses one district per half-day and does not let Subway convenience erase walking and collection scale.

title: Central Glasgow, Merchant City & the Clyde
summary: Start at the station serving the first district, complete one civic or collection anchor, descend through Merchant City or the grid, and finish along a bounded Clyde section.
keywords: Central Glasgow, Merchant City & the Clyde

title: West End, Kelvingrove & the University
summary: Arrive by Subway or bus, complete one museum, cross Kelvingrove Park or the university once, and finish around Byres Road or the Botanic Gardens.

title: Loch Lomond from Glasgow
summary: Leave Glasgow for one gateway, assess water and hill weather, complete one shore, boat or lower-walk plan, and return before branch frequency narrows.

title: Inverness & the Scottish Highlands
summary: Inverness and Loch Ness, Glencoe and Fort William, and Aviemore with the Cairngorms use long, weather-sensitive rail and road corridors. Distances, daylight and sparse alternatives make one named landscape per day the useful maximum. A hotel booking does not make a mountain road, path or cruise operational.

title: Inverness & Loch Ness
summary: Begin on the River Ness, use one verified bus, tour or boat to the selected loch site, and return to Inverness before rural frequency or cruise operation becomes the edge.

title: Glencoe & Fort William
summary: Leave the rail or coach town for one verified glen stop, assess conditions at low level, complete a bounded route or visitor-centre day, and recover the return before road delay compounds.

title: Aviemore & the Cairngorms
summary: Arrive by rail, use Aviemore as the service point, move to one named Cairngorms gateway, and complete a route that can be shortened before the final return.

title: Skye, Orkney & the Outer Hebrides
summary: Skye, Orkney and Lewis with Harris are not one archipelago circuit. They use different ferries, flights, road distances and weather patterns. A credible island plan chooses one system, preserves a mainland or gateway buffer and never treats a booked room as evidence that the crossing or onward bus will operate.

title: Isle of Skye Road & Weather Plan
summary: Start from Portree or another named base, read live road and weather conditions, complete one peninsula or lower-risk island route, and return before darkness or a ferry deadline.
keywords: Isle of Skye Road & Weather Plan

title: Orkney Mainland & Neolithic Sites
summary: Establish the Kirkwall or Stromness gateway, complete one monument cluster with current booking and access, and keep the return crossing or island bus outside the final minute.

title: Lewis & Harris
summary: Enter through Stornoway or Tarbert, use one island half as the day’s operating field, complete a named site cluster, and return before sparse transport or ferry check-in controls the evening.

title: Cardiff, Bannau Brycheiniog & Gower
summary: Cardiff’s civic centre, castle and bay form a rail-and-bus city system. Bannau Brycheiniog and the Gower Peninsula require different gateways, road or bus connections and weather decisions. A strong South Wales stay uses the capital as a base but does not imply the national park or coast begins at Cardiff Central.

title: Cardiff Castle, Civic Centre & Bay
summary: Start at Cardiff Central or Queen Street, complete the castle and civic core or museum, then move once to Cardiff Bay and return by a direct line.

title: Bannau Brycheiniog Gateways
summary: Travel to Brecon, Abergavenny, Merthyr Tydfil or another named gateway, assess mountain conditions there, complete one signed route and recover the final transport before dark.

title: Swansea & the Gower Peninsula
summary: Use Swansea as the rail-and-bus base, travel to one named Gower village or bay, complete a bounded coast route, and return before sparse evening service.

title: Pembrokeshire & West Wales
summary: St Davids, Tenby and the Ceredigion coast sit on separate West Wales corridors. Rail reaches Tenby and Aberystwyth, while St Davids needs a bus or road connection. Coast-path sections, boats and island visits add weather, tide and final-service decisions that should be explicit.

title: St Davids & the Pembrokeshire Coast
summary: Arrive in St Davids, descend to the cathedral precinct, then commit to one signed coast, harbour or boat branch only when weather and return transport remain secure.

title: Tenby, Caldey & the South Coast
summary: Walk from Tenby station into the walled town, read the harbour’s live boat status, complete one island or coast line, and regain the station before the branch service narrows.

title: Aberystwyth & the Ceredigion Coast
summary: Arrive at Aberystwyth station, complete the town and promenade spine, then add one hill, collection or booked heritage-rail branch with the final train protected.

title: North Wales & Eryri
summary: Conwy and Llandudno, Eryri’s mountain gateways, and Caernarfon with Anglesey form three distinct North Wales systems. Rail follows the coast, while mountain routes and castles add buses, seasonal railways, parking and weather. One named gateway per day is the practical standard.

title: Conwy Castle & Llandudno
summary: Begin at the station nearest the main anchor, complete the castle or headland, take one rail or bus connection, and finish on the second town’s compact public realm.

title: Yr Wyddfa Gateway Choice
summary: Reach Llanberis, Pen-y-Pass or another named start, read mountain conditions, complete the booked railway or mapped route with turnaround rules, and return before the gateway transport closes.

title: Caernarfon & Anglesey
summary: Use Caernarfon’s castle and waterfront as one complete field, then cross to Anglesey only for a named town, coast or heritage site with a protected return.

title: Belfast, Causeway Coast & Derry
summary: Belfast’s civic quarters and Maritime Mile are urban transit days; the Causeway Coast is a rail-and-bus or road corridor; Derry is a separate walled city whose recent history requires careful, site-led interpretation. Combining them works across several nights, not as a single highlights loop.

title: Belfast Civic Quarter & Maritime Mile
summary: Begin at City Hall and the central grid, complete one history or civic anchor, then move once to the Titanic Quarter or remain with the city-centre evidence.

title: Giant’s Causeway & the Causeway Coast
summary: Travel from Belfast or a coast base to the visitor route, complete the causeway with official access guidance, then add one named town or viewpoint only when the return remains secure.

title: Derry Walls, Bogside & River Foyle
summary: Arrive at the bus or rail gateway, complete a one-direction wall circuit, descend for one context-rich institution, and finish at Guildhall or the Peace Bridge.
